questions.q: According to Leovy, why did violence become an accepted way to settle disputes?
a: No proper state legal system was ever established there
Residents rejected every form of organized justice
Courts were too expensive for most families to use
Local leaders preferred to settle matters privately
questions.why: Lesson 1 traces it to a history of discrimination and the absence of a trusted legal system.

questions.q: Why is being called a snitch so dangerous in the neighborhoods Leovy describes?
a: A street justice system has replaced official law there
Residents fear their reports will be ignored by police
Witnesses are usually offered money for testimony
Police rarely ask residents for any information
questions.why: Lesson 1 says being a snitch is treated as a death sentence under the law of the street.

questions.q: What is wrong with the LAPD's focus on prevention?
a: It punishes small crimes while murders go unsolved
It spends too much money on detective units
It ignores petty crime in wealthy districts
It relies too heavily on community tips
questions.why: Lesson 2 says prevention drains resources from detectives while punishing people for trivialities.

questions.q: How do mass arrests for minor offenses affect victims' families?
a: They deepen disrespect for a force that ignores violence
They make families more willing to cooperate
They reduce the number of murders in the short term
They free up detectives to focus on bigger cases
questions.why: Lesson 2 says families resent punishment for small things when real violence goes unaddressed.

questions.q: What does Leovy say would restore faith in the legal system?
a: Solving murders equally, whatever the victim's race
Hiring more officers to patrol the streets
Investing in youth programs and job training
Publishing clearer statistics on local crime
questions.why: Lesson 3 argues that solving more murder cases would signal that all citizens matter equally.
